title: Sorted output is not a sufficient contract
stem: A routine returns a nondecreasing array of the same length and sum as its input. Does this prove that it sorts? Construct a counterexample and give a sufficient specification.
solution: No. For input $[0,2,4]$, output $[1,1,4]$ is nondecreasing and has the same length and sum, but replaces two records by different values. Even adding equal minimum/maximum does not suffice: $[0,1,3,4]$ and $[0,2,2,4]$ satisfy those checks. A sufficient contract requires nondecreasing keys and preservation of the full record multiset, including multiplicity and payload identity. For swaps, preservation follows operation by operation. For saved-key insertion, count occupied slots together with the held record; for merging, prove that consumed records are emitted exactly once. This strengthens the inductive hypothesis rather than using a numerical checksum as a proof.
origin: CMU 15-122 Lecture 7, Exercise 1: independently reconstructed contract problem

title: A cyclic comparator invalidates the proof
stem: A comparator on $a,b,c$ states $a<b$, $b<c$, and $c<a$. Explain why increasing sorting under this rule is ill-defined, and distinguish it from a partial-order prerequisite problem.
solution: If a linear order satisfied every stated strict comparison, it would place $a$ before $b$, $b$ before $c$, and $c$ before $a$, which is impossible. Transitivity is violated. A sorting proof that infers that a prefix minimum precedes every suffix record cannot use this comparator. A partial order may instead leave some pairs incomparable; if it is acyclic it can be extended by a topological order. That requires graph dependencies and does not make the given comparator a valid total preorder. Consistent equivalence classes can support stable key sorting, but a cycle between strict classes cannot. Algorithm choice does not repair an inconsistent specification.

title: Selection can reverse keys it never compares as equal
stem: Run minimum-to-front selection on $[2_a,2_b,1_c]$, using the leftmost minimum and suppressing self-swaps. Give the final identity order, comparisons and writes.
solution: The first scan compares the two twos, then compares one with the one: two comparisons identify index two. Exchanging indices zero and two gives $[1_c,2_b,2_a]$, costing two array writes. The next suffix comparison sees equal keys and retains index one, so no exchange occurs. The final order is numerically correct but reverses $a,b$. Total comparisons are three, swaps one and writes two. Choosing the leftmost minimum did not prevent a displaced prefix record from jumping across its equal partner. Stability is about the entire history of record movement, not just the tie chosen by the minimum scan.
origin: CMU Lecture 7 Exercise 5: labeled counterexample reconstructed and solved
visualScope: Exact stated input and variant; full written derivation remains authoritative.

title: Correct priority in stable multipass sorting
stem: Records arrive as $(p,s,id)=[(2,1,a),(1,2,b),(2,0,c),(1,1,d)]$. Produce primary-$p$, secondary-$s$ ascending order using two stable passes. Explain why the reversed pass order solves a different problem.
solution: First sort by secondary key: the stable order is $c,a,d,b$ because secondary keys are $0,1,1,2$, with $a$ before $d$ on the tie. Then sort by primary: the order becomes $d,b,c,a$, with tuples $(1,1),(1,2),(2,0),(2,1)$. Inside each primary block, the prior secondary order survives by stability. If the last pass is instead on $s$, it makes $s$ the highest-priority key, and records with different primary keys can be mixed according to secondary values. The last global stable pass establishes the most significant priority. Sorting by a direct tuple comparator yields the same desired order without separate passes.

title: Turning an unstable sorter into a stable result
stem: Decorate each record with its original index and apply an unstable comparison sorter to $(key,index)$. Prove the result is stable with respect to key, and state the storage/comparison qualifications.
solution: For unequal keys, lexicographic tuple order uses the key, so the result is numerically sorted. For equal keys, tuple order uses the distinct original indices; the earlier occurrence has the smaller index and must appear first. All decorated tuples are distinct, so the underlying algorithm cannot reverse two equal tuples to defeat this argument. If indices are stored in a parallel array or copied record wrapper, that additional storage is typically linear and must be included. Comparing two decorated tuples can need a secondary index comparison after a key tie. The transformation produces a stable result, but it does not make the original undecorated swapping algorithm intrinsically stable.

title: A growing insertion cutoff changes the bound
stem: A balanced divide-and-conquer sorter stops at disjoint subarrays of length at most $k$ and insertion-sorts each. Derive a worst-case upper bound in $n,k$; compare fixed $k$ with $k=\sqrt n$.
solution: Above the cutoff there are $O(\log(n/k))$ linear-work levels, contributing $O(n\log(n/k))$. If cutoff block lengths are $m_i\le k$ and sum to $n$, their insertion work obeys $\sum_i O(m_i^2)\le O(k\sum_i m_i)=O(nk)$. Thus an upper bound is $O(n\log(n/k)+nk)$, with the logarithm interpreted as zero when the cutoff covers the whole array. A fixed cutoff adds only linear leaf work and preserves the usual $O(n\log n)$ bound. Taking $k=\sqrt n$ allows $O(n^{3/2})$ insertion work, which dominates logarithmic-level work. A tuning constant cannot silently become an input-dependent parameter.

title: Selection comparison and movement counts
stem: For an eleven-record input, what comparison count does the specified selection algorithm always make? Give the greatest number of nontrivial exchanges and explain why sorted input changes only movement.
solution: The suffix lengths are ten through one, so $C=10+9+\cdots+1=55$. There are ten outer iterations and each can perform at most one nontrivial exchange, so exchanges are at most ten and array writes at most twenty. A suitable cyclic permutation can require an exchange on every iteration. Sorted input makes every chosen minimum already occupy the target slot, giving zero nontrivial exchanges, yet the scan still inspects every suffix and makes all fifty-five comparisons. An implementation that counts self-swaps would report extra exchange calls without changing its key-comparison count. This separates input-insensitive searching from input-sensitive movement.
visualScope: Exact stated input and variant; full written derivation remains authoritative.

title: Weighted costs can favor a quadratic method
stem: Sorting $n$ large records costs $\alpha$ per key comparison and $\beta$ per array write. Compare a worst-case selection bound with saved-key insertion on an input with $I$ inversions. State a sufficient inequality favoring selection under these bounds.
solution: Selection has weighted upper estimate $\alpha n(n-1)/2+2\beta(n-1)$. Saved-key insertion has exact writes $I+n-1$ and comparisons at most $I+n-1$, but at least $I$. A sufficient bound comparison is $\alpha n(n-1)/2+2\beta(n-1)<\alpha I+\beta(I+n-1)$; then even selection\'s upper bound is below insertion\'s lower bound under this model. For reverse distinct keys, $I=n(n-1)/2$ and insertion comparisons are exactly $I$, so large write cost can make selection preferable despite both methods being quadratic in ordinary runtime. For few inversions insertion can still win strongly. Do not use a worst-case estimate as an exact measured cost on an arbitrary supplied array.

title: Stable selection trades exchanges for shifts
stem: The stable minimum-to-front variant removes a minimum and shifts intervening records right. On reverse distinct input of length $n$, derive its shift and total insertion-write counts.
solution: At iteration zero the minimum is at the final slot, so $n-1$ records are shifted and the minimum is inserted once. The remaining suffix is still in reverse order. Subsequent shift counts are $n-2$ down to one. Total shifts are $n(n-1)/2$ and the $n-1$ selected-record placements add $n-1$ writes, for $W=n(n-1)/2+n-1$ when the final singleton needs no placement. Relative order within every shifted interval is preserved; choosing the earliest minimum preserves the order of equal minima. The original selection method\'s linear exchange bound therefore does not transfer to this stable variant, even though their minimum-scan comparison counts agree.

title: Permutation cycles bound arbitrary swaps
stem: A known distinct-key permutation of six slots has disjoint cycle lengths three, two and one relative to its sorted positions. What is the minimum number of arbitrary exchanges needed? Why is an inversion lower bound inappropriate?
solution: A cycle of length $m$ can be corrected by $m-1$ swaps with a chosen anchor. Summing gives $(3-1)+(2-1)+(1-1)=3$. For a lower bound, one transposition changes the permutation\'s cycle count by at most one, while the sorted identity has six cycles and the given permutation has three. At least three transpositions are necessary. An inversion count instead bounds adjacent exchanges because each adjacent inverted swap removes only one inversion. A long-distance swap can change many inversions at once, so substituting $I$ would generally overstate the arbitrary-swap minimum. The cycle argument assumes the target positions of distinct records are fixed.

title: Exact insertion with an equal key
stem: Use the saved-key strict-$>$ insertion code on $[7_a,3_b,5_c,3_d,2_e]$. Find shifts, key comparisons, array writes and final identities. Count failed key tests explicitly.
solution: The per-insertion shifts are $1,1,2,4$, totaling eight strict inversions. The first and last records inserted become new prefix minima, so those scans stop at the boundary without a failed key comparison. The other two scans stop on a valid predecessor, adding two failed tests. Therefore $C=8+2=10$ and $W=8+4=12$. The final identity order is $e,b,d,c,a$, or keys $[2,3,3,5,7]$. Record $d$ stops after the earlier equal three $b$, demonstrating stability. The model reports shifts 8, comparisons 10 and writes 12; the written count comes from inversions and stopping positions.
visualScope: Exact stated input and variant; full written derivation remains authoritative.

title: Reverse insertion is an exact extreme
stem: On seventeen distinct keys in reverse order, find exact saved-key insertion comparisons, shifts and array writes. Explain the absence of failed key tests.
solution: Insertion at index $i$ crosses all $i$ predecessors, because the new key is the new strict minimum. Thus comparisons and shifts both sum to $1+\cdots+16=136$. Every scan reaches index zero; short-circuit evaluation stops at the bounds test, so no additional failed key comparison is counted. Sixteen held-key placements add sixteen writes, producing $152$ array writes. Runtime remains quadratic even though the key is held in constant auxiliary storage. Counting a failed comparison against a nonexistent index $-1$ would be a bounds error, not an operation in the specified program.

title: Expected inversions with a fixed multiset
stem: A uniformly random permutation of eight labeled records has key multiplicities four, two and two. Find its expected strict inversion count.
solution: There are $\binom82=28$ unordered pairs of labeled records. Equal-key pairs number $\binom42+\binom22+\binom22=8$ and never form strict inversions. Each of the remaining twenty unequal-key pairs appears in either relative position order with equal probability; exactly one order is an inversion. Linearity of expectation therefore gives ten. The distinct-key formula $n(n-1)/4=14$ would incorrectly count half of the eight equal pairs. Record identity is relevant to the random permutation model, while strict inversion compares only keys. No independence among pair events is needed.

title: Binary insertion does not remove quadratic writes
stem: Binary insertion uses upper bound to insert descending distinct records of length $n$. Derive comparison and movement bounds and determine whether its total RAM runtime is $O(n\log n)$.
solution: The prefix of length $i$ has $i+1$ insertion gaps. A balanced binary search finds its upper-bound gap using $O(\log(i+1))$ key comparisons, summing to $O(n\log n)$. The descending new record still belongs before all $i$ previous records, which must each move one slot in a contiguous array. Thus total shifts are $n(n-1)/2$ and held-key writes add $n-1$. With constant-cost writes this implies $\Theta(n^2)$ worst-case runtime. This method helps when comparisons are particularly expensive relative to moving records, but an improvement in one counted primitive is not automatically an improvement in total runtime.

title: Prefix minima account for missing failed tests
stem: For a distinct sequence with $I=19$, length $n=9$, and three inserted records that are new strict prefix minima, find the exact saved-key insertion comparison count and writes.
solution: Every inversion causes one successful key comparison and one shift. There are eight outer insertions. Three move all the way to zero, so their loop terminates on the bounds check; the other five terminate after one failed predecessor comparison. Hence $C=19+5=24$. Each insertion finally writes its held record, so writes equal $19+8=27$. The number of prefix minima includes only inserted records, not the initial first record. Adding nine instead of eight, or adding a failed key test after a boundary stop, counts operations that are not executed. This formula assumes the stated strict comparison implementation.

title: Upper bound versus lower bound changes stability
stem: Insert record $2_c$ into the sorted prefix $[1_a,2_b,2_d,4_e]$. Compare upper-bound and lower-bound placements, and identify the stable placement relative to the incoming history.
solution: Upper bound returns index three, the first key greater than two. The result is $[1_a,2_b,2_d,2_c,4_e]$, preserving both earlier equal records before the newly arriving one. Lower bound returns index one, the first key at least two, and gives $[1_a,2_c,2_b,2_d,4_e]$, which reverses the original relative order between the new record and its equal predecessors. Both outputs are numerically sorted. Binary search\'s strictness condition is therefore part of the stability proof, not merely an optimization. Its exclusive upper boundary can validly equal the prefix length.

title: A rotated sorted block has a calculable inversion count
stem: For distinct ascending blocks, consider $A=[k+1,\ldots,n,1,\ldots,k]$. Derive its inversion count and saved-key insertion shift count.
solution: Neither block contains an internal inversion because each is increasing. Every record in the first block is greater than every record in the second block and appears before it, so every cross pair is inverted. There are $(n-k)k$ such pairs, giving $I=k(n-k)$. Saved-key insertion removes each exactly once and therefore uses that many shifts. If $k=1$, movement is linear despite a cyclic shift of the entire original sorted array. If $k$ is a fixed positive fraction of $n$, movement is quadratic. A visual impression that there are only two sorted runs does not determine the inversion count; it is a different structural parameter.
visualScope: Illustration at n=7, k=3; the symbolic proof applies to the general family.

title: One large misplaced record
stem: For $[n,1,2,\ldots,n-1]$, derive insertion shifts and shrinking early-exit bubble passes. Contrast its mirror arrangement.
solution: The first record exceeds each later record, so there are $n-1$ inversions. Insertion shifts it once while inserting each later key, giving linear movement and comparisons. A left-to-right bubble pass carries the large record all the way to the final slot in $n-1$ comparisons. The next pass has no swap and permits termination, except for tiny arrays whose active prefix already has size one. In the mirror $[2,3,\ldots,n,1]$, the small final record travels left only one slot per forward pass. The same $n-1$ inversion count can then accompany quadratic comparisons. Equal swap counts do not force equal discovery costs.
visualScope: Illustration at n=7; the written proof gives the general n-dependent cost.

title: Few inversions do not make forward bubble linear
stem: Find exact comparisons for forward shrinking bubble on $[2,3,\ldots,n,1]$ with early exit. Explain why the flag does not help asymptotically.
solution: On the first pass, all early adjacent pairs are ordered until the final pair moves the one left by a single slot. On each later pass the one again moves left by one slot; every pass contains an exchange until it reaches zero. The comparison lengths are $n-1,n-2,\ldots,1$, summing to $n(n-1)/2$, although total exchanges equal only $n-1$. The no-swap flag cannot stop any of these passes. This is a concrete separation between the adaptive insertion bound $\Theta(n+I)$ and a superficially similar adjacent-swap sorter. A reverse-direction pass would let the small key move much farther in one pass.
visualScope: Exact stated input and variant; full written derivation remains authoritative.

title: Bubble checkpoints and exact counters
stem: Apply the specified early-exit shrinking bubble to $[4,1,3,2]$. Give each completed pass, comparisons, swaps and writes.
solution: Pass one makes three comparisons and produces $[1,3,2,4]$, using three swaps as four crosses one, three and two. Pass two makes two comparisons; it leaves one before three, swaps three and two, and produces $[1,2,3,4]$. Pass three compares one with two, finds no exchange, and stops. Total comparisons are six, swaps four and writes eight. The four strict inversions of the original array are $(4,1),(4,3),(4,2),(3,2)$, independently checking the swap count. The model agrees with 6 comparisons and 4 swaps. The final no-swap pass still costs a comparison.
visualScope: Exact stated input and variant; full written derivation remains authoritative.

title: Worst comparisons of one gap pass
stem: For $n=11$ and gap $h=4$, compute the largest possible key-comparison count of one ordinary insertion pass over the residue classes.
solution: Write $11=2\cdot4+3$. Three residue classes contain three slots each, and one contains two slots. A reverse-distinct subsequence of length three needs $\binom32=3$ insertion comparisons; the length-two class needs one. Therefore the maximum is $3\cdot3+1\cdot1=10$. Each class can be independently reverse ordered to attain this one-pass bound. The formula is $r\binom{q+1}2+(h-r)\binom q2$. It does not establish the maximum of an entire multi-gap history, because a preceding pass changes the arrays on which the next pass operates. Count comparisons in the actual residue-class subsequences rather than pretending each insertion shifts one adjacent slot.

title: Shell instability across residue classes
stem: Shell-sort $[2_a,2_b,1_c]$ with gaps two then one. Can strict comparisons inside each pass guarantee stability?
solution: The gap-two class at indices zero and two contains $[2_a,1_c]$. Its insertion pass moves the one to zero and the original $2_a$ to two, giving $[1_c,2_b,2_a]$. The gap-one pass sees sorted keys and leaves this identity order unchanged. Thus the equal twos have reversed despite strict comparisons in every residue-class insertion. They belonged to different classes during the long-distance move, so an earlier equal record could leap over its partner without directly swapping an equal pair. Stability of each subsequence sorter does not imply stability of the combined gap sorter.
visualScope: Exact stated input and variant; full written derivation remains authoritative.

title: Gap sorting without a final unit gap
stem: The array $[1,3,2,4]$ is two-sorted. Does this mean it is fully sorted? What termination condition on a Shell gap sequence guarantees ordinary order?
solution: Its even-index subsequence is $[1,2]$ and its odd-index subsequence is $[3,4]$, both sorted. Nevertheless the adjacent pair three then two is inverted. Two-sortedness constrains slots separated by two, not adjacent slots. A final gap-one insertion pass establishes $A_i\le A_{i+1}$ for every adjacent pair and therefore full ascending order under a transitive comparator. A sequence omitting one may accidentally sort some inputs but lacks that general guarantee. The proof should identify the last pass\'s invariant instead of relying on decreasing gaps alone.
visualScope: Exact stated input and variant; full written derivation remains authoritative.

title: Summing separate maxima can be non-tight
stem: An analyst adds the worst comparison count of each Shell pass, computed independently on reverse-ordered residue classes. Is the sum a valid upper bound? Is it necessarily attainable?
solution: Each pass is bounded by its independent worst case regardless of what the earlier passes did, so adding these bounds gives a valid upper bound on the total. Attainability is another claim: the first pass can remove exactly the disorder that the second pass\'s worst-case construction needs. To establish a tight total, one input must realize the relevant high costs in the sequential history, or a lower-bound family must be constructed. Without that witness, write an upper bound rather than a Theta claim. This same logical distinction appears when summing worst loop-branch counts or using the maximum merge cost for a particular supplied array.

title: Exact merging of unequal runs
stem: Merge $L=[1,4,7]$ and $R=[2,3,6,8]$ by comparing heads until one empties. Count key comparisons, and identify the tail copied without a comparison.
solution: The compared winners are one from left, two from right, three from right, four from left, six from right, and seven from left. After these six comparisons the left run is empty. The remaining right eight is copied without another key comparison. Output is $[1,2,3,4,6,7,8]$, and six equals the worst bound $3+4-1$. The sequence of winners justifies the exact count; the bound alone would not prove that this input attains it. Each comparison has two available heads, while the final copy has only one, so charging that copy as a key comparison changes the stated model.
visualScope: Exact stated input and variant; full written derivation remains authoritative.

title: Merge bounds when one run is much shorter
stem: For run lengths two and six, give the best and worst ordinary head-merge comparisons, and compare them with the information lower bound.
solution: The shorter run can empty after two comparisons if both its keys precede every key in the longer run, so the best count is two. Keeping both runs nonempty until the penultimate output gives at most and attainably seven comparisons. There are $\binom82=28$ possible interleavings; the binary information lower bound is $\lceil\log_2 28\rceil=5$. This does not say every input needs five comparisons, and it does not imply the ordinary head-merge implementation is optimal for unequal runs. Its worst seven exceeds that lower bound; a lower bound also need not be attainable by a legal comparison strategy. Movement still involves all eight output records.

title: Exact worst merge comparisons for a non-power of two
stem: Floor/ceiling top-down merge sort processes ten distinct keys. Compute the attainable worst front-merge comparison count without replacing ten by a power of two.
solution: Here $h=\lceil\log_2 10\rceil=4$, so $M(10)=10\cdot4-16+1=25$. Independently, $M(5)=M(2)+M(3)+4=1+3+4=8$, and $M(10)=2\cdot8+9=25$. The top merge uses nine; each child\'s interleaving can attain its own worst count under a suitable recursive rank arrangement. Substituting $10\log_2 10-10+1$ is invalid because that expression was derived only for exact powers of two. A recurrence with rounded child sizes is needed for exact small-instance arithmetic, even when all versions have the same asymptotic order.

title: Best and worst unoptimized merge on sixteen keys
stem: Find best and worst key comparisons of ordinary equal-split merge sort on sixteen distinct records. Does the best count establish linear runtime?
solution: There are four merge levels. In the best case each level costs half the total number of records, so $B(16)=(16/2)\cdot4=32$. The worst count is $16\cdot4-16+1=49$. Sorted input attains the best front-comparison count because every left run empties before any right key is emitted. Conventional merging nevertheless copies all records at each level, which costs $\Theta(16\log_2 16)$ in the general family. A linear runtime on sorted input requires a boundary-skip implementation that also avoids the copying. A question asking comparisons is not interchangeable with a question asking total RAM operations.

title: Empty runs and sentinels use different models
stem: One merge input is empty and the other has seven records. State comparisons and output movement. Then explain why a sentinel merge might report one comparison per emitted record.
solution: With an explicit emptiness check, the comparison loop never starts: key comparisons are zero, but seven records must still be copied or relinked into the output under the stated representation. A sentinel version supplies a fictitious head beyond every legal key and can execute a key test for each output slot, even after a real run empties. Its count therefore differs. The sentinel must be distinguishable from every valid key and must not be copied as a real record. If the allowed universe contains the chosen sentinel value, sortedness and multiset preservation can fail. Never add tail-copy operations to a head-comparison count unless the implementation actually compares them.

title: Right-first ties break stable merging
stem: Merge labeled sorted runs $L=[1_a,2_b]$ and $R=[1_c,2_d]$, formed from consecutive original ranges. Compare left-first and right-first equality rules.
solution: Left-first produces $[1_a,1_c,2_b,2_d]$. Within each child the order is already stable, and across children every original left record preceded every original right record, so choosing left on equal heads retains that history. Right-first instead produces $[1_c,1_a,2_d,2_b]$, reversing both cross-child equal pairs while leaving numerical keys sorted. Correct merge order alone does not prove stable merge order. A backward merge filling the output from the right needs the opposite directional tie choice: on equality choose the right child for the later slot. Tie rules must be interpreted with output direction.
visualScope: Exact stated input and variant; full written derivation remains authoritative.

title: Strict cross-inversions ignore equal heads
stem: For $L=[1,3,3]$ and $R=[2,3,4]$, compute cross-inversions and describe the merge contribution rule.
solution: Only each left three paired with the right two is strict, for a total of two. When the right two is emitted ahead of the first left three, two left records remain, so adding their count records both cross pairs at once. On equal threes, taking a left head adds zero; equality does not satisfy the strict inversion definition. The merge rule adds remaining-left length only when the right head is strictly smaller. If a problem asks nonstrict pairs, change both that definition and the tie branch, rather than reusing this strict count. Sorted child runs justify that every remaining left key exceeds the emitted smaller right head.
visualScope: Exact stated input and variant; full written derivation remains authoritative.

title: A full inversion decomposition
stem: Compute $I([5,2,4,2,1])$ by internal-left, internal-right and cross pairs using the floor split after two elements.
solution: The left $[5,2]$ has one inversion. The right $[4,2,1]$ has three. Cross pairs are five against four, two and one, and the left two against the right one: four. The equal twos do not contribute. Thus the total is $1+3+4=8$. An independent pair list has four inversions from five, one from the first two, two from four and one from the second two, again eight. These pair categories are disjoint and exhaustive, proving the merge-based decomposition rather than merely observing its result on one array.
visualScope: Exact stated input and variant; full written derivation remains authoritative.

title: Boundary skip on a sorted non-power-of-two input
stem: A shared-buffer range merge sorter checks the child boundary and skips all copying on success. On thirty-one ascending keys, find exact boundary comparisons and merges actually performed.
solution: The split recursion has thirty-one singleton leaves and thirty internal nodes because a full binary split tree with $n$ leaves has $n-1$ internal nodes. Every internal node finds the left maximum no greater than the right minimum, so it makes one boundary comparison and performs no merge. Total key comparisons are thirty. Range recursion and checks visit linear many nodes, so runtime is linear, assuming child data were not copied before the check. A slicing implementation that creates both child arrays in advance can still copy logarithmic levels of data. The precise implementation is essential to the adaptive conclusion.
origin: Princeton Mergesort structured-input and skip themes, independently reconstructed
visualScope: Illustration of boundary skipping on eight keys; the question proves the thirty-one-key count from the full recursion-tree invariant.

title: Peak storage differs from cumulative allocation
stem: For $n=64$, a merge sorter allocates a length-$m$ buffer at every nonleaf call before recursively sorting children, releases it on return, and executes children sequentially. Find cumulative buffer cells and peak live buffer cells.
solution: Six nonleaf levels each allocate a total of sixty-four cells, so cumulative allocation is $64\cdot6=384$ cells. At peak descent, simultaneously live parent buffers have lengths $64,32,16,8,4,2$, totaling $126$. Sibling branches do not coexist because recursion is sequential and returned buffers are released. The asymptotic peak is therefore $\Theta(n)$, while cumulative allocation is $\Theta(n\log n)$; recursion frames add logarithmic storage. A single reusable shared array uses sixty-four buffer cells instead. Allocating buffers only after child returns can further change the exact live sum without changing the main linear-space order.
origin: Princeton Mergesort allocation poll, expanded independent derivation

title: Bottom-up final short runs
stem: List run lengths merged at each width for bottom-up merge sort on thirteen records. Explain why the last unmatched run must be retained.
solution: At width one, six pairs of one merge into length two and one singleton remains: $2,2,2,2,2,2,1$. At width two, three pairs of twos merge into fours and the singleton remains: $4,4,4,1$. At width four, the first two fours form eight, and the next four plus singleton form five: $8,5$. At width eight, those runs form thirteen. Exclusive endpoints use minima with the array length. Dropping an unmatched run would violate permutation preservation even if all produced runs were sorted. The pass invariant permits shorter final runs; it never requires padding the input with fake records.

title: A sorted prefix and a short unsorted tail
stem: An $n$-record array has a sorted prefix of length $n-\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor$ and an arbitrary remaining tail. Give a worst-case linear-time sorting approach in the comparison model and justify the bound.
solution: Sort the tail with merge or heap sorting in $O(\sqrt n\log n)$ time, then merge it with the sorted prefix in $O(n)$ time. Since $\sqrt n\log n=O(n)$ for sufficiently large $n$, the total is $O(n)$. The input family already supplies substantial ordering information, so the unrestricted $\Omega(n\log n)$ lower bound does not forbid this. If stability is required, use stable tail sorting and left-first merging. Simply running a conventional merge sort over every record ignores the promise. A lower bound on reading or emitting all records gives linear order under the ordinary complete-output model.
origin: Princeton Mergesort structured-array problem, independently reconstructed

title: An unbalanced run schedule can be quadratic
stem: There are $r=n$ singleton runs. Compare sequentially merging the current accumulated run with the next singleton against balanced merging; count total emitted records.
solution: Sequential merge output lengths are $2,3,\ldots,n$, so total emitted records are $n(n+1)/2-1=\Theta(n^2)$. This copying cost persists even if key comparisons become cheap on a specially ordered input. Balanced merging has logarithmic levels and emits at most $n$ records per level, for $O(n\log n)$ output work. A natural merge sorter must therefore specify its merge schedule; detecting sorted runs alone does not establish an adaptive complexity bound. Inserting each singleton by binary search can reduce comparison work but still requires shifting or building the accumulated output in an array representation.

title: Descending-run reversal needs strictness
stem: A run detector accepts $[3_a,3_b,2_c]$ as weakly decreasing and reverses it. Is that operation compatible with a stable complete sorter?
solution: Reversal yields $[2_c,3_b,3_a]$, already numerically sorted but with the two threes reversed. No later stable sorting pass can restore their original order from keys alone. A stable run-reversal method can safely reverse strictly decreasing runs because they contain no equal-key pair. Alternatively it needs a special equal-block repair or different representation with original indices. The local detector\'s nonstrict comparison changes the global stability argument. This counterexample is small enough to check directly and separates numerical monotonicity from record identity preservation.

title: Sorting bounded displacement
stem: Every distinct record is at most $k$ positions from its final sorted index. Prove why a min-heap of the next $k+1$ records can emit the next sorted record, and state time/space.
solution: When emitting sorted index $i$, its correct record originally lay at an index no later than $i+k$ by the displacement promise. Earlier emitted records have already been removed; scanning through $i+k$ ensures that this record is among the retained candidates. A minimum of those candidates is therefore the next globally remaining key. Remove it, add the next unread record, and repeat. Heap operations cost $O(\log(k+1))$ for $k\ge1$, giving $O(n\log(k+1))$ time and $O(k+1)$ space; for $k=0$ the already sorted input is processed directly in linear time. An inversion bound is a different promise and does not automatically imply this displacement value.

title: Exact Lomuto partition and recursive comparisons
stem: Sort $[4,1,5,2,3]$ using strict-$<$ Lomuto with the last record as pivot in every half-open range. Derive the first partition and the total key comparisons.
solution: The first pivot is three. Scanning four leaves it in the large block; one swaps to the front; five remains large; two swaps into the next small slot. The final pivot exchange yields $[1,2,3,4,5]$, with the pivot at index two and child ranges $[0,2)$ and $[3,5)$. This first partition uses four comparisons. Each length-two child uses one comparison, giving six total. The fact that the first partition happened to order both children does not skip those calls in the unoptimized code. Self-swaps may be suppressed in movement counts, but the scan comparisons still execute. A different scan partition can produce different child orders and exact totals.
visualScope: Exact stated input and variant; full written derivation remains authoritative.

title: Random pivots do not cure strict Lomuto duplicates
stem: Use strict-$<$ Lomuto quicksort on eight equal keys, selecting a random pivot record before moving it to the last slot. Find comparisons and explain whether randomness yields the distinct-key guarantee.
solution: Every nonpivot key fails the strict less-than test. The partition therefore puts the pivot at the first slot, leaving children of lengths zero and seven. The same event occurs recursively regardless of which equal record was selected. Comparisons sum to $7+6+\cdots+1=28$. Randomness changes identities and exchanges, but not these child lengths. The usual harmonic expected-comparison formula assumes distinct ranks and is not applicable. Three-way partition would remove the entire equal block in one pass, while a correctly implemented equal-stopping inward scan can obtain balanced divisions with logarithmic levels.
visualScope: Exact stated input and variant; full written derivation remains authoritative.

title: Classic Hoare returns a boundary, not a pivot slot
stem: Apply the taught classic Hoare split to $[4_a,1_b,3_c,2_d]$. Give its returned index and array, then derive the two recursive ranges.
solution: With saved pivot value four, the left scan stops at the first four and the right scan stops at the final two. Exchanging them gives $[2_d,1_b,3_c,4_a]$. The next left scan reaches the final four and the next right scan reaches the three; indices cross and the algorithm returns $j=2$. The pivot occurrence is at index three, not at the returned index two. The correct half-open children are $[0,3)$ and $[3,4)$. Omitting slot two as though it were a finalized pivot is not justified. The contract only separates keys on the two sides of the returned boundary and ensures a shrinking split; it does not identify a pivot position.
visualScope: Exact question input; only its first Hoare partition is executed.

title: Child lengths must conserve records
stem: A proposed quicksort recurrence after removing one pivot is $T(n)=2T(n-\sqrt n)+\Theta(n)$. Explain the structural defect and write the recurrence for a guaranteed smaller side of approximately $\sqrt n$.
solution: The two proposed child lengths total $2n-2\sqrt n$, exceeding the available $n-1$ nonpivot records for large $n$. Ordinary partition produces disjoint children; records cannot belong to both, so this recurrence cannot describe that quicksort split. If one side is about $\sqrt n$, the other is about $n-1-\sqrt n$. Suppressing rounding and the pivot constant gives $T(n)=T(\sqrt n)+T(n-\sqrt n)+\Theta(n)$. A recurrence question should first check conservation, then the selection guarantee and toll. Two large branches would describe a different algorithm that deliberately revisits or duplicates data, not ordinary partitioning.

title: An exact randomized expectation
stem: For ideal uniform-pivot quicksort on five distinct keys, compute the expected key-comparison count exactly, and compare it with the worst case.
solution: The harmonic number is $H_5=1+1/2+1/3+1/4+1/5=137/60$. Thus $\mathbb E[C_5]=2\cdot6\cdot137/60-20=37/5=7.4$. The worst pivot chain uses $4+3+2+1=10$ comparisons. The expectation need not be an integer because it averages integer counts over random executions. It counts one pivot-versus-nonpivot comparison per record in each partition and excludes additional sampling or scan-crossing tests. The derivation by indicators, or the recurrence averaged uniformly over the five possible pivot ranks, establishes the expression without substituting an average child length into a nonlinear cost function.
origin: Stanford CS161 Lecture 5 pair-indicator analysis, independently calculated instance

title: Probability that two ranks are ever compared
stem: In ideal randomized quicksort with distinct ranks, find the probability that ranks three and eight are compared. Why are pivots outside this interval irrelevant to the event?
solution: The rank interval contains six records: three through eight. The pair remains together until a pivot from that interval is selected. A pivot outside it puts both ranks into the same child and cannot separate them. If the first selected interval rank is three or eight, that pivot is compared with the other endpoint. If it is four through seven, the endpoints enter different children and never meet again. All six ranks are equally likely to be first under uniform random priorities, so the probability is $2/6=1/3$. The argument depends on sorted ranks, not their physical original indices.

title: Balanced expectation can conceal one-sided executions
stem: A pivot algorithm chooses the minimum or maximum uniformly at each call. Compute expected child lengths, then derive runtime. Identify the incorrect expectation substitution.
solution: The two possible splits are $(0,n-1)$ and $(n-1,0)$, so each labeled child has mean length $(n-1)/2$. Nevertheless every execution has one nonempty child of length $n-1$. With a linear partition toll, the recurrence is $T(n)=T(n-1)+\Theta(n)$, giving $\Theta(n^2)$. Selecting the extremes by an extra linear scan keeps that same order. The invalid step is replacing $\mathbb E[T(|L|)]$ with $T(\mathbb E[|L|])$. Balanced means describe no actual execution here. The correct uniform-pivot analysis averages over every rank or uses pair indicators, rather than analyzing an imagined average-sized split.
origin: Stanford CS161 Lecture 5 SlowSort counterexample, independently reconstructed

title: Probability of a completely extreme pivot chain
stem: For five distinct keys with independent uniform pivot choices in each current range, find the probability of choosing an extreme rank at every nontrivial call.
solution: At range size $m\ge2$, exactly two of the $m$ ranks are extremes. Conditional on all previous choices being extreme, only one nontrivial child remains, of size $m-1$. Multiply conditional probabilities: $(2/5)(2/4)(2/3)(2/2)=2/15$. In general the probability is $\prod_{m=2}^n2/m=2^{n-1}/n!$. Every such execution has the maximal ideal comparison sum $n(n-1)/2$. The small probability does not make worst-case time disappear, nor does it justify claiming that a randomized execution always meets a fixed deadline. This event calculation assumes distinct keys and the stated uniform conditional choices.

title: Median of three is a local rank promise
stem: A deterministic pivot is the median of three sampled distinct keys. Give its guaranteed global rank interval and explain why it need not produce a fixed-fraction split.
solution: One sampled record is below the median and one above, so the pivot\'s zero-based global rank lies between one and $n-2$. There is no stronger guarantee from only these three records: every unsampled record can be above the pivot, making one child length one and the other $n-2$. This is not a fixed fraction bounded away from zero as $n$ grows. Random sampling can improve average balance under its probability model, but the deterministic sample guarantee alone still permits a long unbalanced family. Derive pivot guarantees from known sample ranks, not the word median without its sample size.

title: A larger sample has a limited worst guarantee
stem: Choose the median of eleven distinct sampled records out of thirty. What smallest side is guaranteed? If the sample is sorted by insertion, bound its worst comparison cost and first partition cost.
solution: The sample contains five smaller and five larger keys, so each child contains at least five records and at most twenty-four, since their lengths total twenty-nine. The unsampled nineteen records can all lie on one side, so five versus twenty-four is attainable. Reverse-order insertion of the eleven sampled keys costs $11\cdot10/2=55$ comparisons. An ideal full partition then compares its twenty-nine nonpivot records with the chosen pivot. A selection method may use fewer comparisons, but that is a different pivot-finding implementation. The sample guarantee does not imply a fifteen-versus-fourteen split of all thirty records.

title: Exact-median pivot gives a worst-case guarantee
stem: Assume a deterministic linear-time exact-median subroutine and partition preserving distinct records. Derive the full quicksort worst-case runtime, including median computation.
solution: Median finding and partition together cost $\Theta(n)$ per range. The exact median gives children of lengths $\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor$ and $\lceil(n-1)/2\rceil$. Therefore $T(n)=T(\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor)+T(\lceil(n-1)/2\rceil)+\Theta(n)$, whose balanced tree has logarithmic depth and linear work per level, giving $\Theta(n\log n)$. It is incorrect to omit median finding because it is a real operation, although its linear order fits the same toll. This construction establishes a deterministic bound; practical constant factors and selection implementation details are separate questions developed in the selection chapter.

title: Smaller-first is insufficient without tail iteration
stem: An implementation recursively sorts the smaller child first and then recursively sorts the larger child. Does this guarantee logarithmic stack depth on one-sided partitions? State the correct transformation.
solution: No. When one child is empty, its recursive call returns immediately, but the larger child is still entered recursively while the parent activation remains live. Repeating yields a chain of linear many active calls. Instead recurse only on the smaller child and handle the larger child by updating bounds in a loop inside the current activation. Every actual nested recursive call then enters a range of size at most half the preceding range, so there are $O(\log n)$ simultaneous activations even on a quadratic-time pivot history. Merely ordering recursive calls does not remove the parent frame. Runtime and storage guarantees must be proved independently.

title: Timing evidence cannot alone prove an exponent
stem: When the input size is multiplied by four, one measured sorting time grows about fivefold and another about eightfold. A researcher declares exact $n\log n$ and $n^2$ laws. What can be inferred, and what remains unproved?
solution: If an exact dominant $cn\log_2n$ law applied, the ratio would be $4(1+2/\log_2n)$, tending toward four. An exact dominant $cn^2$ law would give sixteen, not eight. The observations can motivate hypotheses, but constants, lower-order terms, measurement setup, caching and input families can distort finite ratios. Big-O alone does not assert equality with one monomial. Under the special promise that two known implementations differ only in fixed-first versus random pivot and are tested on sorted distinct inputs, relative degradation can help identify the fixed-pivot implementation, but still is not a general asymptotic proof. Derive the recurrence from the algorithm before claiming a Theta law.
origin: CMU Lecture 7 Exercise 6 timing interpretation, independently reconstructed with explicit inference limits

title: A faithful deterministic-middle counterexample
stem: Use the exact CMU scan partition, with middle index pivot, on $[1,3,5,7,6,4,2]$. Verify a worst-case seven-record comparison chain; do not borrow Lomuto intermediate states.
solution: The successive nontrivial pivot values in the CMU implementation are seven, one, six, five, two and four. Their final pivot slots are respectively six, zero, five, four, one and three in the current ranges. Every partition leaves one empty child, so range lengths are seven down to two. Each scan classifies each nonpivot once, giving $6+5+4+3+2+1=21$ comparisons. The first pivot seven moves to the end, but its initial swap changes the next middle record; claiming that the next pivot is automatically six would not follow this actual code. This example proves that choosing a middle physical index need not choose a middle rank.
origin: CMU Lecture 7 Exercise 3: source input with independently corrected trace
visualScope: Exact stated input and variant; full written derivation remains authoritative.

title: Temporary partitioning can still be unstable
stem: A partition copies keys at most the pivot to the left of a temporary array and larger keys from right to left into its right end. Does extra memory guarantee stability? Design a stable alternative.
solution: No. Two larger equal records encountered in original order are written into successively decreasing right positions, reversing their order in the resulting large-key block. Extra storage makes stability possible but does not enforce it. A stable alternative scans original records once and appends to three FIFO sequences: less, equal and greater. Concatenating those sequences retains identity order within every comparison class and preserves all records. The extra output storage is linear in the range length and key classification is linear. To establish stable quicksort, recursive child sorts must also be stable; one stable partition does not repair an unstable child method.
origin: CMU Lecture 7 Exercise 4 temporary-memory partition, independently strengthened

title: Three-way region boundaries on a concrete input
stem: Apply the taught three-way partition with first pivot to $[3_a,1_b,3_c,5_d,2_e,3_f,4_g]$. State the first final regions and the total comparator count of complete three-way sorting.
solution: The first pivot value is three. The first final array is $[1_b,2_e,3_c,3_f,3_a,4_g,5_d]$, with less range $[0,2)$, equal range $[2,5)$ and greater range $[5,7)$. Six nonpivot records are classified in that partition. Each two-record unequal child then uses one ternary comparator call, for eight in the whole sorting execution. The equal records finish in order $c,f,a$, which reverses the original $a,c$ pair, so the method is not stable. When a large record swaps with the unexamined right boundary, the scan index does not advance, because its imported value still needs classification.
visualScope: Exact stated input and variant; full written derivation remains authoritative.

title: All-equal three-way work and strict tests
stem: On twelve equal records, how many ternary comparator invocations, swaps and nontrivial recursive children does the taught three-way version use? Compare with two Boolean tests per invocation.
solution: The initial equal region contains the pivot. Each of the other eleven records returns equality and advances the scan. There are eleven logical ternary comparator invocations, no swaps and no nontrivial recursive children because the complete equal block spans the input. The expression `(v > pivot) - (v < pivot)` implements that invocation using two Boolean key tests, so that primitive model counts twenty-two tests. Both are linear, but their exact constants differ. One cannot compare eleven ternary calls directly with twenty-eight Boolean strict-Lomuto tests from a different size or implementation. Define the counted primitive before interpreting counters.
visualScope: Exact stated input and variant; full written derivation remains authoritative.

title: Fixed distinct-value count versus dominant frequency
stem: Compare inputs with at most seven distinct keys against inputs where 99% of records have one key and the remaining keys are unrestricted. Does either promise imply linear worst-case comparison sorting?
solution: Three-way quicksort has at most seven partition levels on the first family because each path removes one distinct value. Total work per level is at most linear, so this implementation has $O(7n)=O(n)$ worst-case work, with input processing giving linear order. In the second family the remaining $n/100$ keys can all be distinct. Embed an arbitrary order of those keys among identical fillers and recover their sorted order after sorting the full array. A hypothetical linear comparison algorithm would then sort arbitrary distinct arrays in linear time after constant-factor padding, contradicting the lower bound. A dominant frequency is not a fixed bound on the number of distinct values.
origin: Princeton Quicksort duplicate-key and Mergesort common-key problems, independently reconciled

title: Heap indexing is a representation theorem
stem: For a zero-based complete binary heap of length thirteen, list children of index five, the parent of index twelve, the leaves, and the last internal node.
solution: Children of five are eleven and twelve, both below thirteen. The parent of twelve is $\lfloor(12-1)/2\rfloor=5$. Internal indices satisfy $2i+1<13$, giving indices zero through five. Leaves are six through twelve, and the last internal node is $\lfloor13/2\rfloor-1=5$. These formulas refer to the complete-tree array layout, not arbitrary binary trees. During sortdown the active heap length can be smaller than the full array length, so child validity must use that active length; the sorted suffix must never reenter sink. One-based formulas $2i,2i+1$ would address different physical slots.

title: Floyd construction and exact sortdown
stem: Use the specified larger-child sink and Floyd construction on $[4,10,3,5,1]$. Give the built heap, construction comparisons and total heapsort comparisons.
solution: Process internal node one first: choose five over one and compare ten with five, using two comparisons and no swap. At node zero, choose ten over three, compare four with ten and swap; at node one choose five over one, compare four with five and swap. Construction uses six comparisons and gives $[10,5,3,4,1]$. Sortdown then uses three, two, one and zero comparisons in active heaps of lengths four, three, two and one. Total comparisons are $6+3+2+1=12$. The final array is $[1,3,4,5,10]$. Exact counts include child selection, not just parent-versus-child checks.
visualScope: Exact stated input and variant; full written derivation remains authoritative.

title: The sum of node heights is small
stem: For a complete heap with thirty-one nodes, compute the sum of all node heights and a construction comparison upper bound using at most two comparisons per descent level.
solution: The number of nodes with height at least one is fifteen; with height at least two, seven; then three and one. Summing gives $15+7+3+1=26$. Charging two comparisons per available level gives at most fifty-two construction comparisons. This is an upper bound, because some sinks stop early or have only one child at a level. It is less than $2n=62$. Counting height by thresholds avoids an off-by-one error in the number of nodes at each exact height. Multiplying thirty-one by the root height four gives a valid but loose estimate and does not reveal linear construction.

title: Top-down construction is a different operation history
stem: For increasing distinct keys one through eight, compare individual max-heap insertion construction with the specified Floyd construction. Count only construction comparisons.
solution: Each newly inserted key is the largest and swims all the way to the root. Its number of ancestor comparisons is $\lfloor\log_2i\rfloor$ for one-based insertion count $i$. Summing for $i=1,\ldots,8$ gives $0+1+1+2+2+2+2+3=13$. Floyd instead sinks internal nodes three, two, one and zero; its counts are one, two, three and four, totaling ten. Both produce valid heaps but generally different intermediate arrays. The distinction becomes $\Theta(n\log n)$ versus $\Theta(n)$ construction in worst-case families. Heapsort\'s later extraction phase is not included in these construction-only numbers.
visualScope: Exact stated input and variant; full written derivation remains authoritative.

title: All-equal heapsort can be linear
stem: Use the taught early-stop sink on seven equal keys. Find construction and total comparison counts, and explain why this does not contradict heapsort\'s worst-case bound.
solution: Each of the three internal nodes has two children, so construction makes two comparisons at each and stops immediately: six. After each root/end exchange, active lengths are six, five, four, three, two and one. Root sinking then uses two, two, two, two, one and zero comparisons, totaling nine. The whole execution has fifteen comparisons and six nontrivial root/end swaps, with no downward swaps. Keys being equal makes every parent pass the early-stop condition. Worst-case $\Theta(n\log n)$ means there exist inputs requiring that order, not that every input has it. The specified all-equal family takes linear work.
visualScope: Exact stated input and variant; full written derivation remains authoritative.

title: Heap order does not preserve equal identities
stem: Heapsort $[2_a,2_b,1_c]$ with the taught max-heap code. Is the result stable? Why does initially valid heap order not resolve the question?
solution: The initial array is already a max-heap, so construction leaves it alone. Moving the root $2_a$ to the last slot gives $[1_c,2_b,2_a]$. Sinking the one swaps it with $2_b$, giving $[2_b,1_c,2_a]$. The final extraction yields $[1_c,2_b,2_a]$. Equal identities are reversed, so this method is not stable. Heap order constrains parent keys versus child keys and says nothing about original chronological order among equals. A valid heap can therefore be the starting point of an unstable sortdown. Decorating keys with original indices can enforce the target order but changes the comparison and storage model.
visualScope: Exact stated input and variant; full written derivation remains authoritative.

title: An integer decision-tree lower bound
stem: What integer worst-comparison lower bound follows from sorting six distinct keys using binary pair comparisons? Does that prove a sorter attaining the bound exists?
solution: The tree needs at least $6!=720$ leaves. Since $2^9=512<720\le1024=2^{10}$, its height is at least ten. The conclusion is a lower bound: every correct tree must have some path of at least ten comparisons. It does not construct an attainable sorting tree, and arbitrary balanced binary questions might not be legal pairwise comparisons of records. Nor does it say every input takes ten comparisons. To prove optimality for a small fixed size, a legal sorting construction and a matching lower bound are both needed.

title: Multiplicity changes the leaf count
stem: Known key multiplicities are four, two and two in eight slots. Compute the distinct-arrangement count and binary-comparison leaf lower bound; compare with all-distinct keys.
solution: The count is $8!/(4!2!2!)=420$. Binary height is at least $\lceil\log_2 420\rceil=9$, because $256<420\le512$. With eight distinct keys, the count is $8!=40320$ and the corresponding bound is sixteen. Equal keys reduce the number of possible key arrangements; labeled record identities still matter for stability but do not create additional unknown key orders inside a known equal group. The model counts binary decisions; a primitive three-outcome comparison can require a different constant-base branching calculation on inputs with ties. Bounds apply to the stated input family and primitive.

title: Merging has less unknown order than sorting
stem: Two internally sorted distinct runs have lengths two and six. Explain the $\binom82$ arrangement count and why the unrestricted $8!$ sorting count is wrong.
solution: The internal order of each run is already fixed. An output is determined by choosing the two positions occupied by records from the first run; the other six positions are filled by the second run in its known order. Thus there are $\binom82=28$ possible interleavings, not $8!$. The binary leaf lower bound is five comparisons. Applying an unrestricted distinct sorting bound would count internal run permutations that the precondition excludes. Ordinary merging can still use seven comparisons on a worst supplied interleaving. Information lower bounds constrain the best possible worst-case strategy, while the cost of one particular strategy can be larger.

title: Lower-bound quantifiers and a sorted input
stem: An examiner states: every comparison sorter must use $\Omega(n\log n)$ time on an already sorted input. Refute the statement with a correct algorithm and state the valid bound.
solution: Insertion sort with a strict predecessor test checks each new record against its immediate predecessor, makes $n-1$ key comparisons, shifts nothing and completes in linear time on ascending input. It is nevertheless a correct sorter for arbitrary inputs, with a quadratic worst case. The valid theorem says every correct comparison sorter has a worst-case input family requiring $\Omega(n\log n)$ comparisons when arbitrary distinct relative orders are allowed. The theorem does not specify that the hard input is ascending, nor claim that every input is hard. A supplied promise that the input is already sorted can reduce the task further; reading or verification requirements must then be stated.

title: Randomness cannot erase the general average lower bound
stem: A randomized comparison sorter is always correct. Outline why some fixed distinct-key input must require expected $\Omega(n\log n)$ comparisons.
solution: Fix a sequence of random coins. The resulting correct deterministic sorting tree must distinguish all $n!$ relative input orders. Under a uniform distribution over them, average leaf depth is at least $\log_2(n!)$. Average that inequality over the algorithm\'s random coins, exchanging the finite input average and expectation. The average across fixed input orders of their expected costs remains at least $\log_2(n!)$. At least one fixed input must therefore have an expected cost no smaller than that average. This is a lower bound for always-correct comparison sorting; it does not contradict a randomized algorithm having matching expected upper bounds on every fixed input.

title: An unsorted tail does not require sorting the prefix again
stem: A million records contain a known sorted prefix and one thousand arbitrary trailing records. Give a stability-preserving comparison strategy and its asymptotic expression.
solution: Stably sort the thousand-record tail, using $O(1000\log_2 1000)$ work, then perform a stable left-first merge with the known sorted prefix in $O(10^6)$ work. More generally the expression is $O(n+k\log k)$ for a tail of size $k$. The known prefix reduces the unknown-order family, so the unrestricted comparison lower bound is not a barrier. If the records carry payloads, use complete records in the tail sort and output merge. Applying counting sort based solely on the record count would need an additional bounded-integer-key promise; it is not implied by the sorted-prefix information.

title: Stable cumulative scatter positions
stem: Count-sort records $[3_a,1_b,3_c,0_d,2_e,1_f]$ in universe zero through three. Compute frequencies, cumulative ends and the final identity order.
solution: Frequencies are $F=[1,2,1,2]$, whose cumulative ends are $P=[1,3,4,6]$. Scanning right to left, $1_f$ goes to slot two, $2_e$ to three, $0_d$ to zero, $3_c$ to five, $1_b$ to one, and $3_a$ to four. Output is $[0_d,1_b,1_f,2_e,3_a,3_c]$. Each block receives exactly its frequency count; decrementing ends cannot overlap adjacent blocks. The later equal record takes the later slot first, so original equal order survives. All six output writes place distinct original records, while counter updates are separate storage operations rather than key comparisons.
visualScope: Exact stated input and variant; full written derivation remains authoritative.

title: A mixed scatter convention reverses ties
stem: Use cumulative end positions but traverse $[2_a,1_b,2_c,1_d]$ left to right, decrementing the end for each record. What identity order results, and how can the convention be repaired?
solution: Frequencies are two ones and two twos, with exclusive ends two and four. Left-to-right traversal places $2_a$ at three, $1_b$ at one, $2_c$ at two and $1_d$ at zero. Output is $[1_d,1_b,2_c,2_a]$, reversing both equal groups. To repair it while retaining ends, traverse the original records right to left. To retain left-to-right traversal instead, compute starting positions zero and two and increment them after each placement. Both corrected conventions give $[1_b,1_d,2_a,2_c]$. The off-by-one is not merely numerical: traversal direction and pointer direction jointly establish stability.

title: Negative keys need the range width
stem: Stably count-sort $[-3_a,2_b,-1_c,2_d,-3_e]$ with interval $[-3,2]$. What counter array size is required and what is the final identity order?
solution: The inclusive width is $2-(-3)+1=6$. Shift each key by subtracting $L=-3$: indices are zero, five, two, five, zero. Frequencies are $[2,0,1,0,0,2]$ and cumulative ends are $[2,2,3,3,3,5]$. Right-to-left scatter gives $[-3_a,-3_e,-1_c,2_b,2_d]$. Allocating only three counters because the maximum is two ignores negative indices and the full interval width. Stability preserves both pairs of equal identities. Shifting changes representation used for indexing, not the actual payload or key that must be returned.
visualScope: Exact stated input and variant; full written derivation remains authoritative.

title: Sparse occupancy does not shrink a dense universe
stem: There are one thousand records but only four occupied key values, all inside an interval of width one billion. Is ordinary dense counting sorting linear in one thousand? What extra work appears in a sparse replacement?
solution: Ordinary dense counting initializes and scans one billion counters, so its cost is $\Theta(n+K)$ and its storage includes $K$, despite only four occupied values. A sparse map can record frequencies or FIFO record groups for the four keys in near-linear scanning time under an appropriate dictionary model. To emit them in ascending key order, the occupied keys must themselves be ordered, for example by comparing and sorting those four keys; dictionary iteration is not automatically ordered. If the number of distinct keys varies, this gives a distinct-value sorting term and dictionary assumptions. Low occupancy and small universe are different conditions, and neither alone eliminates representation cost.

title: Counts-only reconstruction loses payloads
stem: A counting routine emits integer key $j$ exactly $F_j$ times. Applied to records $(key,name)$, does it establish a stable record sort? Describe what must be stored instead.
solution: It reconstructs only the numerical key multiset; names and other attached fields have been discarded. Calling the output stable is therefore meaningless for the original records, and the record permutation contract is violated. Store each complete record in a FIFO key bucket or retain the original array and scatter complete records into cumulative positions. Then prove every occurrence is output exactly once and equality retains original order. If the input really consists solely of indistinguishable integer values, counts-only reconstruction is a legitimate integer sorting variant. The validity depends on the input contract, not on the algorithm\'s shared counting-sort name.
origin: Oxford B16 counts-only variant versus MIT stable-record variant, independently synthesized problem

title: Three exact LSD decimal passes
stem: Sort $[329,457,657,839,436,720,355]$ using stable LSD base-ten passes. Give the complete array after each pass and justify the final order.
solution: The units pass yields $[720,355,436,457,657,329,839]$: equal units seven retain 457 before 657, and equal units nine retain 329 before 839. The tens pass yields $[720,329,436,839,355,457,657]$: the prior order resolves each equal tens bucket. The hundreds pass yields $[329,355,436,457,657,720,839]$. After one pass the units are sorted; after two, the two-digit suffix is sorted; after three, every full three-digit key is sorted. Buckets are concatenated in digit order and preserve FIFO identity order. Sorting digits independently without that stability invariant would not justify these arrays.
origin: MIT 6.006 Recitation 5 Exercise 1: exact written exercise with independently explained solution
visualScope: Exact stated input and variant; full written derivation remains authoritative.

title: An unstable digit pass invalidates LSD
stem: After a stable units pass on $[12,11]$, an unstable tens sorter reverses equal tens. Give the resulting array and identify the broken invariant.
solution: The units pass puts eleven before twelve, giving $[11,12]$, correctly sorted by the low digit. Both tens are one. Reversing that equal tens bucket then produces $[12,11]$, which is not numerically sorted. The next-digit pass must preserve the established lower-suffix order among equal next digits; instability removes precisely that property. It is not enough that each individual digit list appears sorted after its pass. A correct LSD proof compares two keys by the new digit first and, when that digit ties, relies on their previous suffix order. This two-record counterexample isolates the missing condition.

title: Global MSD-then-LSD passes solve the wrong priority
stem: Globally sort $[21,12]$ first by tens and then stably by units. Does this implement numeric order? Contrast recursive MSD.
solution: The tens pass gives $[12,21]$. A global units pass then gives $[21,12]$, because one precedes two, so numeric order is lost. The last stable pass becomes the highest-priority key when passes are global. Recursive MSD avoids this by sorting lower digits only within each equal high-digit bucket. Here the tens buckets each contain one record, so no later pass can mix them. The distinction is between refining a fixed high-priority group and reordering the entire array by a lower-priority component. Pass direction alone is not a complete algorithm specification.

title: Inclusive and exclusive universe boundaries
stem: With base two, compare digit counts for keys below exclusive $U=1024$ and keys up to inclusive $M=1024$. Explain why a floating-log shortcut can be unsafe.
solution: Keys below 1024 have maximum 1023 and need ten binary digits because $2^{10}=1024$ covers the exclusive universe. The inclusive maximum 1024 itself is binary one followed by ten zeros, so it needs eleven digits. Thus $d=\lceil\log_2U\rceil$ for the first case and $d=\lfloor\log_2M\rfloor+1$ for the second. Treating the same numeric bound as both inclusive and exclusive gives an off-by-one at exact powers. Floating-point logarithms near a boundary can also round incorrectly; repeated integer division or a tested place-value loop computes the required pass count exactly.

title: A bit-length ratio is not an exact arbitrary-base digit count
stem: For base $B=n=3$ and exclusive universe $U=59049=3^{10}$, evaluate $1+\lfloor\operatorname{bitlength}(U)/\operatorname{bitlength}(n)\rfloor$. Is that enough passes for key $U-1$?
solution: The universe 59049 has binary bit length sixteen, while three has bit length two. The proposed expression gives $1+\lfloor16/2\rfloor=9$. But $U-1=59048$ has ten base-three digits, all two, and nine passes cannot inspect its highest digit. The ratio of rounded binary lengths is not the exact logarithm in base three. Use the minimum integer $d$ satisfying $3^d\ge U$, which is ten, or repeated integer division. Approximate formulas acceptable for some asymptotic estimates must not become exact implementation bounds without a proof. This independently checked edge case motivated the chapter\'s explicit digit loop.
origin: MIT radix implementation audit: newly authored correction and counterexample

title: Linear radix on a shifted polynomial interval
stem: Design a word-RAM linear-time method for integers in $[-n^2,n^3]$, with $n\ge2$. Bound the required base-$n$ digits after a monotone shift.
solution: Add $n^2$ to each key, producing nonnegative values at most $n^3+n^2$. For $n\ge2$, this maximum is less than $n^4$, so at most four base-$n$ digits suffice. Perform four stable counting digit passes with $n$ counters each, costing $O(n+n)$ per pass and $O(n)$ peak extra storage when buffers are reused. Retain original complete records or subtract the shift after sorting values. The shift is monotone, preserving order. The constant four and the word-size arithmetic assumption are essential; arbitrary huge integers can invalidate a constant-cost operation model. For a singleton, handle the base-one issue by returning directly.
origin: MIT Recitation 5 Exercise 2: reconstructed and strengthened with exact boundaries

title: Digit width trades memory for passes
stem: For a million unsigned 64-bit keys, compare dense radix work estimates with eight-bit and sixteen-bit digits. Explain why thirty-two-bit digits can be infeasible.
solution: Eight-bit digits require eight passes and 256 counters, giving proxy work $8(1000000+256)=8002048$. Sixteen-bit digits need four passes and 65536 counters, giving $4(1000000+65536)=4262144$. Under this simplified equal-cost proxy the sixteen-bit option is smaller, but actual cache behavior and counter initialization constants still matter. Thirty-two-bit digits need only two passes yet require $2^{32}$ counters, which is billions of entries and can exceed available memory. The general formula is $\lceil64/b\rceil(n+2^b)$ with peak buffer plus counter storage, not just the number of passes. A memory constraint can override the arithmetic proxy.

title: Encoded size changes a claimed linear bound
stem: Keys have up to $n$ bits, and a radix analysis chooses base $n$. Why must the arithmetic model be specified when reporting $O(n^2/\log n)$ digit work?
solution: A key needs roughly $n/\log_2n$ base-$n$ digits, so a hypothetical constant-cost digit pass yields $O(n\cdot n/\log n)$ work. But an $n$-bit key generally spans many ordinary machine words. Treating divisions, shifts or comparisons of the whole key as constant-time assumes an unusually large word or hides big-integer cost. Reading the complete encoded input already involves up to $n^2$ bits. The meaningful complexity must specify word width, digit extraction representation and whether input/output are measured in records, words or bits. The formal digit-count expression can be correct while its advertised machine runtime is unsupported.

title: Nonuniform bucket probabilities determine expected work
stem: Independently place $n$ records in buckets with probabilities $p_i$. Derive $\mathbb E[\sum_iN_i^2]$ and evaluate uniform placement into $n$ buckets versus one bucket.
solution: Write $N_i=\sum_{j=1}^nX_{ji}$. Its second moment is $np_i+n(n-1)p_i^2$, because diagonal terms are $X_{ji}$ and independent distinct-record terms have expectation $p_i^2$. Summing and using $\sum_ip_i=1$ yields $n+n(n-1)\sum_ip_i^2$. For $n$ uniform buckets, the squared probabilities sum to $1/n$, giving $2n-1$. For one bucket the sum is one, giving $n^2$. Insertion work within buckets is bounded by this second moment, so independent near-balanced placement can give expected linear time while concentration permits quadratic work. Marginal probabilities alone are insufficient if placements are dependent.

title: A concentrated bucket is a real worst case
stem: Use five equal intervals for integer percentages zero through ninety-nine, and insertion-sort each bucket. Trace $[19,18,17,16,15]$. Does bucket assignment make the sort linear?
solution: All five values lie in the first interval zero through nineteen, so bucket assignment creates one descending five-record bucket and four empty buckets. Its insertion sorter needs $\binom52=10$ strict shifts or adjacent exchanges, with ten successful predecessor comparisons for the specified reverse input. Distribution and concatenation add linear work but do not remove the quadratic internal-sort family when all $n$ inputs similarly concentrate in one bucket. Output is $[15,16,17,18,19]$. The uniform expected-time theorem assumes a distribution of random placements; one deterministic bucket mapping is not evidence that inputs satisfy it.
visualScope: Exact stated input and variant; full written derivation remains authoritative.

title: Strings require an end-of-string order
stem: Lexicographically sort the strings `a`, `aa`, `ab`, and the empty string. Explain the required MSD sentinel and the character-cost qualification for equal-length strings.
solution: The correct order is empty string, `a`, `aa`, `ab`. The end-of-string sentinel must precede every ordinary character, so a completed string comes before any longer string sharing its prefix. At the first character the empty string enters the terminal bucket; at the next character `a` enters it before `aa` and `ab`. Recursion continues only in nonterminal character buckets. For $n$ equal-length strings of length $L$ over alphabet size $R$, stable LSD passes cost $\Theta(L(n+R))$, which is linear in all input characters for fixed $R$, not linear in record count alone. A normal character cannot double as an end sentinel without changing the intended order.
origin: MIT Recitation 5 Exercise 3 and Stanford radix induction: independently extended string problem

title: External merging counts passes and blocks
stem: Let $n=10^6$ records, usable buffer memory after metadata $M=10000$ records, and block size $B=100$. Generate memory-sized sorted runs, then use one input block per run plus one output block. Compute run count, fan-in, merge passes and total read/write transfers including generation.
solution: Run count is $r=\lceil10^6/10000\rceil=100$. The buffer-only fan-in is $f=10000/100-1=99$, with metadata already excluded as stated. One merge pass reduces one hundred runs to two; the second reduces two to one, so there are two merge passes. Each pass reads and writes all records: $2\cdot10000=20000$ transfers. Run generation also reads and writes them once, adding twenty thousand. Total is sixty thousand block transfers under this full-materialization model. CPU head comparisons and final-output omission policies would change other cost terms; they are not included in the stated transfer convention.
